source.title: Explaining neural scaling laws
source.authors: Yasaman Bahri; Ethan Dyer; J. Kaplan; Jaehoon Lee; Utkarsh Sharma

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplemental material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law loss scaling and its dependence on data, architecture and training choices in neural networks, using a different setup from language-model scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper measures population/test loss against dataset size, parameter count or width, mainly in image-classification, teacher-student and feature-model settings. It does not test language-model pretraining loss, scaling with training tokens or compute, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. The cited scaling-law results from other studies are not recorded as rows. Theory-only results and measurements used only to estimate data-manifold dimension are not rows.
record.test_reason: Measures test-loss power laws in dataset size, width and feature count for image CNNs, Wide ResNets, random-feature models and pretrained ImageNet features. That is a new setting for V5, and it varies data, noise, architecture and regularisation, which bears on V7. No language-model pretraining, token/compute sweeps, extrapolation or allocation results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim that resolution-limited exponents reflect the data-manifold dimension: confirmed in teacher-student models, less clear on real data. They find a duality αD=αP=αK in random-feature models, which pretrained features match well. Superclassing leaves the exponent unchanged, which they read as networks learning the input manifold.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and tests a theory of dataset-size and parameter/width scaling in neural networks, random-feature models and pretrained image features; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining scaling or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset distribution and added input noise affect resolution-limited exponents; superclass count has no visible effect; width affects dataset-scaling exponents up to saturation, while depth has a milder effect. Fixed low versus tuned regularization changes the pretrained-feature scaling behavior. The resolution-limited prediction breaks down when the required dataset/model-size hierarchy is lost.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss versus dataset size and loss versus feature count track each other: the D–P duality in random-feature and pretrained-feature models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dataset-size and parameter-size resolution-limited exponents are equal (αD=αP=αK) in linear/kernel regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Resolution-limited exponents scale with the inverse data-manifold dimension (4/αD≈d in teacher-student models; less clear on real data).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling exponents are set by the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold.

fits_no_version.finding: WRN aspect ratio changes the dataset-scaling exponent: width up to a saturating value, depth only mildly. This is not at fixed P.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture aspect ratio affects dataset-scaling exponents.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: The authors state that the theoretical results are asymptotic while experiments use finite models and datasets; the resolution-limited regime requires a size hierarchy and relies on a data-manifold assumption for deep networks. Some reported exponents are presented in figures, and the data-manifold proxies are acknowledged as imperfect.
record.rows_left_out: No results meeting the row criteria were omitted. Language-model scaling, training-token and compute sweeps, small-run extrapolation, and compute-optimal allocation are not tested; cited results from other papers are excluded.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss; no scaling with tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs extrapolated to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
No loss comparison at fixed parameter count across shapes; width and depth vary P.
Video, repeated data, and language-model fine-tuning or transfer are not tested. Only image classification, synthetic teacher-student data and a linear probe on pretrained image features.
Parameter counting, fitting method and the compute-optimal split are not examined; published LM laws are not compared.

missing.what: WRN resolution-limited dataset exponents (αD≈0.26–0.58) and width exponents of the underparameterised depth-10 ResNet (αW≈0.34–0.62) across CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and FashionMNIST
Variance-limited power laws in image networks as evidence of the power-law form (αD≈0.98–1.11, αW≈0.98–1.03)
Final versus best (early-stopped) loss and error give similar scaling, so the metric or stopping choice does not change the trend
Random-feature models on pooled MNIST: resolution-limited αD/αP 0.34–1.31, varying with pool size; variance-limited ≈1.00–1.15
Teacher targets give much larger exponents than real labels for the same features (e.g. αD 2.52 vs 0.25)

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source (different paper, though Kaplan is a co-author). The tranche was changed from T2 to T3 because the evidence comes from new settings (image, synthetic, pretrained features), not a different method on LM loss. The Fig S7 exponent-to-panel mapping is inferred from garbled figure text.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss or scaling with parameters, tokens and compute in language models.
It does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not study fixed-compute allocation between model size and training tokens.
It varies depth and width and reports effects on dataset-scaling exponents, but does not compare loss at fixed parameter count as this version specifies.
The empirical settings include image datasets and pretrained image features, but not video, repeated-data training, or a general survey of fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
It does not test downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.

It examines dependence on dataset, noise, architecture aspect ratio, regularization and asymptotic regime; it does not compare language-model scaling-law fits or compute-optimal splits across fitting methods and training schedules.
